title: What is known about 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_0RB---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_0RB---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. It belongs to a family of four holdouts that share their first four states, and works as two binary counters, one counting down in the blocks left of the head and one counting up in the gaps right of it. This page lists what is established, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. Lean now proves the counter itself: read the tape as two binary numbers, E in the odd blocks left of the head and N in the gaps right of it, and every countdown of E, for every size of E and N, runs as the counter says (run3, run5). Lean also proves that the blank-tape run enters this counter after 160 steps and runs its first countdown. The pass rules (including the halting one) are proved too.

What is not proved is what happens between countdowns. When E runs out the tape is reorganised; the reorganisation leaves defects on the right (gaps of an irregular size, blocks of two 1s), and the machine halts only if such defects meet in one particular way. No invariant excluding this is known. An accelerated simulation, whose jumps are instances of the Lean countdowns, reaches 8.47·101907 steps with no halt and with never more than one defect at a time.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: The pass rules
claims.text: Six rules on symbolic tapes, for all values of their parameters and any surrounding tape: a pass on an even top block (L 1 A>0 1^(2k+4) 0^(g+2) 1 R), on a block of 2, on an odd block crossing j small gaps, on a block of 3, a gap of length one closing, and pass_odd_halt: an odd pass whose D-run meets a gap one cell too short reaches F reading a 1, the only halting transition. Proofs by rfl steps and crossing lemmas, written by tools/py/bbtools/symtm.py.

claims.title: 1a and 1b agree on F0 followed by 0
claims.text: From L x F>0 0 R both 1RB1LA_..._1RB0RF_0RB--- and 1RB1LA_..._1RB0RF_1RC--- reach L A>x 1 1 R in 3 steps (f00_0, f00_1). The two machines differ only when F reads a 0 followed by a 1.

claims.title: The counter, proved for every size
claims.text: Write E in p bits on the left (from the head outward, a 0 bit is 1 1 and a 1 bit is 1 0, above a floor that starts with a 1) and N in n bits on the right (a 0 bit is 0^3, a 1 bit is 0^2 1, followed by any tape X). In mode 3 (top block 1^3) the machine takes (E, N) to (E − k, N + k) for every k ≤ E with N + k < 2n, in at least 22·k steps (run3); in mode 5 (top block 1^5) it takes (E, N) to (E − k, N + 2k) in at least 48·k steps (run5). Proofs: three pass-pair rules written by tools/py/bbtools/symtm.py, the binary decrement and increment on bit lists, and induction on k.

claims.title: The blank-tape run enters the counter
claims.text: After 160 steps from blank tape the machine is in mode 5 with E = 17 (5 bits) and N = 1 (init_counter), and it then counts E down to 0, reaching N = 35 after at least 816 further steps (first_countdown).

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 137 cells have been visited and 63 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 2·10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: Direct simulation with tools/c/tmrun.c. The tape at step 8,593,882,720 (end of the second phase) is exactly the one the accelerated simulator predicts.

claims.title: The counter rule on 4.7 million cycles
claims.text: On the regular shape (head A on 0, 1^5 or 1^3 to its right, then gaps 0^(3q+2) 1) every one of 4,687,473 consecutive cycles of 1a between steps 1,500 and 3·108 takes (E, F) to (E − 1, F + 1) as the two-counter model says, and takes 48 + 4v + 6j steps (v, j read off the top block and the leading gaps). 1a and 1b have the same run here: in their first 109 steps F is entered 6 times, always on a 0 followed by a 0.

claims.title: No halt before 8.47·10<sup>1907</sup> steps
claims.text: The round-2 accelerator py/jump2.py (with c/ps.c, in the folder of 1a) simulates directly from pass start to pass start until the tape is a counter configuration of lean/Counter.lean (top block 3 or 5, E and N readable with at least 12 bits), then jumps a whole countdown at once: k cycles with k up to E (or down to the next power of two) and within the room N has before its first defect. Each jump is an instance of run3/run5, so its end tape is proved; only the Python reading of the tape, the exact step count (fitted formula a + 4ν(E) + 6ν(N+1) per pair) and the direct simulation between jumps are unproved. Jumps of at most 108 steps were each re-run by direct simulation and matched token for token. In 25 minutes on one core it made 245 jumps and reached step 8.47·101907 (E up to 6,452 bits) with no halt.

claims.title: Defects stay single
claims.text: In the 42.1 million passes that the round-2 run of 1a simulated directly (all the transition cascades between its 245 jumps), the right part never held more than one defect, never more than one 1^2 block, the left part never more than two even blocks, and the fatal precursor (a gap one cell short directly followed by a block of two or more) never occurred.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/fixed
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.036).

claims.title: The phase transition
claims.text: When E reaches 0 the floor block 1^(2s) under it is popped into the top block, the next pass pushes s single 1s, and a new countdown starts with E = 2s − 1 (s one bits; floor 1^2) in the other mode (3 and 5 alternate); N stays on the right, but the cut leaves a gap of irregular size in front of it. Irregular gaps then act in a cascade of short sub-phases: a gap one too long (for 1a/1b; the analogous residue mod 5 for 1c/1d) collapses into a block 1^2, a gap one too short followed by a single 1 is cut down and passes its defect on to the next gap; sometimes the whole of N is pulled to the left and N restarts at 0. The floor grows by 2 whenever E passes a power of two, so it is about twice the bit length of the largest E so far. Seen at every transition of the runs above; not proved, and no closed formula for the new (E, N) as a function of the old one is known.
claims.where: holdouts/1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_0RB---/py/jump2.py (log of the tapes at each counter start)

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. By pass_odd_halt the machine halts exactly when an odd pass, after the gaps of the smallest size, meets a gap of length one followed by a block of two or more 1s. In the counter language this needs two defects to meet: an irregular gap cut down to length one directly in front of a 1^2 block left by another defect. During a countdown there are no defects (proved: the countdown is run3/run5), so it can only happen inside a transition cascade. In the runs above there was never more than one defect at a time; no invariant proving that is known, and the transitions have not been reduced to a number-theoretic map.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this Turing machine counts one binary number down and another one up, again and again, in phases that get longer and longer. This page shows the real machine in your browser, explains the two counters, and says exactly where a halt could come from.

facts.text: Proved in Lean, including the only way a pass can halt.
No halt in a validated accelerated run (53 jumps).

sections.heading: Four machines, one engine
html: Four holdouts share the first four states of this machine, 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB, and differ only in the last two: 1a 1RB0RF_0RB---, 1b 1RB0RF_1RC---, 1c 1RF0LE_1RA---, 1d 1RF1RC_1RA---. States A to D do almost all of the work; E and F only decide what happens when the head runs into the right part of the tape. This page is about machine 1a; the other three work the same way with different constants.

In 1a and 1b the gaps on the right have lengths 2, 5, 8, 11, ... (3d + 2); in 1c and 1d they have lengths 4, 9, 14, ... (5d + 4). 1a and 1b even agree step for step as long as F only ever reads a 0 followed by another 0, which is what happens in every run we made.

sections.heading: Blocks on the left, gaps on the right
html: Stop the simulator at a moment when the head is in state A on a 0 with a block of 1s to its right. The tape then looks like
0^∞ 1^(2s) 0 1^(2v1+1) 0 1^(2v2+1) ... A>0 1^m 0^(3q1+2) 1 0^(3q2+2) 1 ... 0^∞

Left of the head: blocks of an odd number of 1s separated by single 0s (and one even block at the far left). Right of the head: single 1s separated by gaps whose lengths are 2, 5, 8, .... The odd blocks and the gaps are the digits of two numbers.

sections.heading: How a block of 1s is used up
html: From such a moment to the next (a pass) the head eats the block 1^m two cells at a time: states A, B and C carry one 1 at a time to the left part, then D runs right and writes into the first gap. What happens depends on m:

• m even: two 1s move to the left, the first gap gets one cell shorter;
  • m odd: D runs right over all the gaps of the smallest size, (0^2 1); those gaps merge into one long gap, and the first larger gap is cut;
  • m = 2 or 3: the block merges with the blocks on its left and the head walks back to the 0 left of them.
These pass rules are proved in Lean for every value of the block lengths and every surrounding tape (lean/Rules.lean).

sections.heading: One number counts down, another counts up
html: Read the tape at the start of a pass as two binary numbers. Left of the head, going outward, every pair of cells is one bit of E, lowest bit first: 1 1 is a 0 and 1 0 is a 1, down to an even block, the floor. Right of the head, after the top block, every group of 3 cells is one bit of N: 0^3 is a 0 and 0^2 1 is a 1. (So an odd block 1^(2v+1) is v zero bits and a one bit, and a gap is a run of zero bits closed by a one bit.)

With top block 1^3 (mode 3) one pair of passes subtracts 1 from E and adds 1 to N; with 1^5 (mode 5) two pairs subtract 1 from E and add 2 to N. A pair costs a constant plus 4 steps per trailing zero of E plus 6 per trailing one of N, exactly the work of borrowing and carrying.

2141^2 0 1^9 A>0 1^5 0^2 1 0^2 1163
This is now proved in Lean for every E and N (lean/Counter.lean: run3, run5), and Lean also proves that the run from blank tape reaches this counter after 160 steps (lean/Init.lean).

sections.heading: When the countdown ends
html: When E reaches 0 the floor 1^(2s) is popped into the top block; the next pass pushes s single 1s, which is E ≈ 2s − 1, all ones, and the mode switches between 3 and 5. N is left on the right, but the pass that cut it leaves a gap of the wrong size, a defect, in front of it.

Defects are worked off in a cascade of short sub-phases: a gap one cell too long collapses into a block 1^2; a block 1^2 followed by a gap makes the next gap one too short; a gap one too short followed by a single 1 is cut and hands its defect to the next gap. Sometimes N is swallowed into the left part entirely and restarts at 0. Then a clean countdown runs again. Since the floor gains 2 cells each time E passes a power of two, the floor is about twice the bit length of the largest E so far, and phases grow fast.

The accelerator py/jump2.py simulates the cascades directly and jumps over every clean countdown with the Lean-proved rule. In 25 minutes on one core it made 245 jumps and reached step 8.47·101907 (E up to 6,452 bits) with no halt.

sections.heading: How it could stop
html: The machine halts only when F reads a 1. From a pass start that happens exactly when an odd pass, after the gaps of the smallest size, meets a gap of length one followed by a block of two or more 1s (pass_odd_halt, proved). In the language above that needs two defects at once: a gap cut down to length one, directly in front of the 1^2 left by another defect. In every transition seen so far a single defect was worked off without harm.

During a countdown there are no defects at all, so a halt can only come inside a transition cascade. In the 42.1 million passes that the round-2 run of 1a simulated directly (all the transition cascades between its 245 jumps), the right part never held more than one defect, never more than one 1^2 block, the left part never more than two even blocks, and the fatal precursor (a gap one cell short directly followed by a block of two or more) never occurred.

sections.heading: What is missing
html: The counter is proved; the transitions are not. A transition is a cascade whose course depends on the low bits of E and N and on where earlier defects sit, and no closed formula for the configuration after it is known, so neither an invariant (“there is never more than one defect”) nor a reduction to a number-theoretic map is available yet. The runs make the one-defect invariant plausible but do not prove it.
Because the phases grow so fast, simulation can only ever check a few dozen transitions; whatever decides this machine has to be an argument about all transitions at once.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.036).
After 109 steps the tape spans 137 cells (6 left of the start, 127 right), with a density of 1s of 0.46.

The tape (run-length coded, 1^5 is five 1s, C>0 the head in state C on a 0) at some of the last moments the head reached a new cell, cut to 400 characters:

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Almost the same run as 1RB1LA_1LC1RD_1LA0LC_1RE0RB_1RB0RF_1RC--- (observed, not proved). Tape and head are the same at all but 12 of the first 107 steps from blank tape. The two runs part 6 times, each time for a step or two and by one cell, first at step 9 and last at step 4,072,133, and come together again. The tables differ and are not renamings of each other. While the runs agree, the states pair up as A–A, B–B, C–C, D–D, E–E, F–F (this machine first).

summary: Family 1a: two binary counters, E written in odd blocks left of the head counting down and N written in gaps right of it counting up (proved in Lean for every size); when E runs out the floor block becomes a new E and defects appear on the right; it halts only if two defects meet. No halt to 8.47·10^1907 steps (accelerated run). Open.
